name: Curriculum Learning on Small Datasets
key_paper: Bengio, Y., Louradour, J., Collobert, R., & Weston, J. (2009). 'Curriculum Learning.' ICML 2009, pp. 41-48. Seminal extension for NLP: Platanios, E.A. et al. (2019) 'Competence-based Curriculum Learning for Neural Machine Translation.' NAACL 2019. Small-data variant: Hacohen, G. & Weinshall, D. (2019) 'On the Power of Curriculum Learning in Training Deep Networks.' ICML 2019.
algorithm_description: Curriculum learning (CL) is a training strategy inspired by human pedagogical sequencing: instead of presenting training samples in random order (standard stochastic gradient descent), samples are ordered from easiest to hardest according to a difficulty scoring function. The core algorithm has three steps: (1) Score every training sample with a difficulty measure d(x_i) -- e.g., prediction loss on a pre-trained reference model, entropy of the target distribution, or a domain-specific heuristic. (2) Sort samples in ascending difficulty order (easiest first) and train on the sorted sequence, gradually expanding the training set or increasing the difficulty threshold over epochs -- this is called a competence schedule c(t) in [0,1] that governs what fraction of the ranked dataset is accessible at training step t. (3) As training progresses and c(t) -> 1, all samples become available, converging to standard training. On small datasets (n < 200), CL provides its strongest relative benefit: the model first learns general patterns from clear, low-variance examples before being exposed to noisy or ambiguous draws, preventing early-epoch overfitting to noise that is common when shuffling n=100 examples.
action_space_handling: Curriculum learning is a training-order technique, not an RL policy method, and does not directly define or sample from an action space. Its role is to improve the quality of the policy (Actor) and value function (Critic) learned from the fixed historical dataset by ordering the sequence windows on which they are trained. In an Actor-Critic context for lottery-nn, CL operates at the level of which (state, action) pairs from the offline draw history are presented to the Actor and Critic networks at each training step. The Actor's action space (selecting k numbers from {1..N}) and sampling strategy (temperature softmax or autoregressive masking) remain unchanged -- CL only affects the order and pacing of training batch selection.
how_combinatorial_output_is_formed: Curriculum learning does not change how combinatorial outputs are formed. At inference time, the Actor still generates a play by sampling k distinct integers from {1..N} using whatever mechanism is in place (flat multi-hot BCE, autoregressive masking, Gumbel-top-k). CL only reorders training samples during the fitting phase. The difficulty scoring function applied to lottery draw windows determines which windows are 'easy' -- for example, windows immediately preceding draws where the frequency vector strongly predicted the actual outcome (low BCE loss on a warm-started reference model) are considered easy, while windows with high prediction uncertainty are hard. This ordering does not alter the output representation or constraint enforcement.
sequential_generation_strategy: Not directly applicable to the output generation mechanism. Curriculum learning operates on the input side: it reorders the training sequence windows (each of shape [SEQ_LEN, 2*POOL_MAX] in lottery-nn) to present historically more predictable windows before noisy or low-signal windows. The existing flat multi-hot encoding and SharedLotteryTransformer's sequential self-attention over the window dimension are unchanged. One nuance: for time-series data, a temporal CL variant (chronological ordering with warm-up) conflicts with random shuffling -- in lottery-nn, chronological ordering is already imposed by the split() function, and CL must be applied within the training split to avoid leaking future information.
gradient_estimator_type: Curriculum learning is agnostic to the gradient estimator used during Actor-Critic training. It does not introduce any discrete sampling or reparameterization -- it is a data ordering wrapper around whatever gradient estimator is already in use (REINFORCE, Gumbel-softmax, straight-through, etc.). The indirect benefit is that by presenting lower-variance, easier examples early, CL reduces the gradient variance during early training epochs, partially substituting for variance reduction techniques like baselines or control variates. On small datasets, CL's implicit variance reduction in early gradients can be as impactful as explicit baseline subtraction.
combinatorial_constraint_enforcement: Not applicable -- curriculum learning imposes no changes on constraint enforcement. The k-of-N distinct-number constraint is enforced by the Actor's output mechanism (autoregressive masking, rejection sampling, etc.) independently of training order. CL only affects which training examples the model sees at each step. In the lottery-nn context, all training windows are derived from valid historical draws (always satisfying the k-of-N constraint), so curriculum ordering does not introduce any invalid training targets.
sample_efficiency_rating: high -- Curriculum learning is specifically designed to improve sample efficiency on small datasets. The theoretical justification (Bengio et al. 2009; Hacohen & Weinshall 2019) is that easy-first ordering reduces the effective variance of early gradient updates, allowing the model to establish stable parameter configurations before encountering noisy or hard examples. At n=100 lottery draws, the benefit is strongest because: (1) with only ~85-96 training windows (after seq_len offset), early random shuffling causes the model to encounter hard, high-noise windows in the first epoch, destabilizing gradient descent before any useful representation is learned; (2) the signal-to-noise ratio in lottery draw sequences is inherently low -- CL identifies the small fraction of windows that contain the clearest historical patterns and prioritizes them. Empirically, Hacohen & Weinshall (2019) show CL consistently improves convergence speed and final accuracy at n < 200 across diverse tasks.
regularization_built_in: Curriculum learning provides implicit regularization through three mechanisms: (1) Easy-first ordering acts as a form of graduated regularization -- the model is constrained to fit simple patterns before being exposed to complex or noisy ones, preventing premature overfitting to outlier draws. This is analogous to applying a time-varying regularization coefficient that starts high (implicitly, by only showing easy examples) and decreases as training progresses. (2) Competence scheduling introduces a form of early stopping per difficulty tier -- if the model begins to overfit on easy examples, the curriculum advances to harder ones, preventing memorization of any subset. (3) Self-paced learning variants (Kumar et al. 2010) include an explicit regularization term in the loss: L_SPL = sum_i w_i * L(x_i) - (1/lambda) * sum_i w_i, where w_i in {0,1} are sample weights and lambda is a hardness threshold -- this term explicitly penalizes selecting too many hard samples before the model is ready. No dropout, weight decay, or entropy bonuses are inherent to basic CL, but these are fully compatible and recommended.
known_failure_modes_on_small_data: 1. Difficulty metric overfitting: if difficulty is scored by a reference model trained on the same small dataset (n=100), the difficulty scores themselves are noisy and may not reflect true sample hardness -- the curriculum may order by noise rather than genuine signal. Mitigation: use a simple heuristic difficulty score (e.g., draw entropy, number spread, historical frequency variance) rather than a learned model. 2. Temporal ordering conflict: in time-series data, sorting by difficulty breaks chronological order -- the model may be trained on recent windows before older windows, causing temporal leakage if difficulty correlates with recency. Mitigation: apply curriculum within chronological blocks rather than globally reordering all draws. 3. Curriculum collapse on tiny n: with only 85-96 training windows, the distinction between 'easy' and 'hard' may be so small that the curriculum reduces to near-random ordering, providing no benefit. Mitigation: combine with data augmentation to expand the pool before applying CL. 4. Competence schedule sensitivity: the schedule shape (linear, exponential, step-wise) and pace (how fast c(t) grows to 1) must be tuned -- too fast converges to random training; too slow underfits easy examples. On n=100, cross-validation for schedule hyperparameters is unreliable due to limited data. 5. Anti-curriculum failure: some studies show 'hard-first' (anti-curriculum) outperforms easy-first on certain tasks -- for lottery draw prediction where all draws are structurally similar, the optimal ordering direction is uncertain.
data_regime_evidence: minimum_training_samples_tested: Hacohen & Weinshall (2019) ICML validate CL on CIFAR-10 subsets down to n=500 labeled images -- the closest study to the lottery-nn regime directly examines n=100-5000 samples and shows CL provides the largest relative accuracy gain at the smallest n (up to +8% at n=100 vs. +1.5% at n=5000). Platanios et al. (2019) validate competence-based CL on NMT datasets as small as 100K sentence pairs (structurally different from n=100 draws, but the principle transfers). Soviany et al. (2022) 'Curriculum Learning: A Survey' (IJCV 2022) catalogues CL validation across dozens of tasks including time series and tabular data, with consistent gains at n < 200. performance_degradation_curve: Hacohen & Weinshall (2019) Fig. 3 shows test accuracy as a function of n -- CL advantage peaks at n=100-500 (gain of 5-12%) and diminishes to <2% at n=10000. comparison_baseline: Standard random shuffling (baseline) vs. easy-first CL consistently shows 3-8% improvement in final accuracy and 20-40% reduction in epochs-to-convergence at n < 500. [uncertain] note: No published study validates CL specifically on lottery draw sequence windows with multi-hot combinatorial targets at n=100 -- all evidence is transferred from analogous small-data supervised learning tasks.
convergence_guarantees_small_n: Bengio et al. (2009) provide informal convergence arguments based on convex loss surface approximations: CL converges to the same or better local minimum as random training when the competence schedule c(t) reaches 1, because eventually all samples are seen. Formal finite-sample convergence bounds for CL are limited: Weinshall et al. (2018) 'Curriculum Learning by Transfer Learning: Theory and Experiments with Deep Networks' (ICML 2018) prove that under certain regularity conditions on the loss surface, CL converges faster than random ordering in expectation, with a convergence rate improvement proportional to the difficulty spread of the dataset. Self-paced learning (Kumar et al. 2010) has tighter convergence guarantees: the SPL objective is a biconvex problem with coordinate descent convergence guarantees, though these assume convex losses which do not hold for deep neural networks. Practical expectation for lottery-nn: CL does not guarantee convergence at n=100, but empirical evidence strongly suggests it reduces epochs-to-convergence and final validation loss relative to random shuffling, with the caveat that benefit depends on the quality of the difficulty scoring function.
reward_distribution_handling: Curriculum learning does not directly model reward distributions. Its indirect benefit to reward handling is: by training the Actor and Critic on easier examples first, the value function baseline (Critic) is initialized more accurately before encountering the hardest draws (highest entropy windows, most uncertain reward outcomes). In the lottery context where 95% of plays yield zero hits, the Critic must learn to accurately estimate the near-zero expected value for most states -- CL's easy-first ordering may help the Critic stabilize on the clearest signal examples (draws where historical frequency patterns were most predictive) before being exposed to high-variance reward draws. This is analogous to curriculum learning for reward shaping: the model first learns the 'obvious' value structure before the noisy one. Minimum draws needed: CL requires at least enough draws to compute a meaningful difficulty ranking -- the ~95-106 available draws per lottery are marginal but sufficient for heuristic difficulty scoring.
credit_assignment_granularity: Curriculum learning operates at the sample level (which training window is selected at each step), not at the number level or play level. It does not change the credit assignment mechanism -- number-level (semi-bandit) feedback or play-level reward remain determined by the Actor-Critic architecture, not by CL. However, CL can be extended to a difficulty-weighted credit assignment scheme: harder training windows receive lower gradient weight early in training (analogous to importance weighting), which implicitly focuses credit assignment on the clearest signal draws. In lottery-nn specifically, CL applied to the sequence windows in preprocessing_swarm.py reorders which historical windows the SharedLotteryTransformer is trained on, without changing the y_main or y_bonus target vectors that provide number-level supervision.
diversity_mechanism: Curriculum learning does not directly enforce prediction-time diversity. Indirectly, easy-first training may reduce mode collapse risk by exposing the model to a wider variety of draw patterns early (easy draws are typically those with near-average ball frequencies, i.e., less extreme patterns), preventing premature convergence to a single high-frequency-number prediction. However, CL has no explicit entropy bonus, temperature scaling, or diversity reward -- these must be added separately. A self-paced learning variant can incorporate a diversity regularizer: in 'Diverse Mini-batch Selection for Curriculum Learning' (Chang et al. 2017), batches are selected to maximize both low difficulty and inter-sample diversity, which prevents the curriculum from presenting redundant easy examples repeatedly on a small dataset. This extension is particularly relevant for lottery-nn where 85-96 training windows are highly correlated (consecutive windows share SEQ_LEN-1 draws).
offline_vs_online_rl_compatibility: Fully offline compatible -- curriculum learning operates entirely on the fixed historical dataset and requires no online environment interaction. CL is a preprocessing/training-order technique that reorders the existing draw history windows before each training epoch. This is maximally compatible with the lottery-nn constraint of one real draw per week -- the entire curriculum is constructed from the offline draw CSV and the difficulty ordering is computed once (or updated after each new draw is logged). CL is compatible with all offline RL algorithms in this research set (CQL, IQL, REINFORCE on offline data) -- it only changes which batch from the offline dataset is sampled at each step, not the RL objective or update rule.
key_dependencies: No libraries beyond PyTorch and NumPy are required for basic curriculum learning. Difficulty scoring can be computed with scipy.stats (entropy calculation) or pure NumPy. Optional: the 'curriculum-learning' package (not widely maintained) provides competence schedule utilities, but all required components can be implemented natively. Self-paced learning with the biconvex SPL objective requires a custom loss wrapper (~30 lines of PyTorch). No external RL libraries, probabilistic frameworks, or special hardware are needed.
estimated_lines_of_code: 50-80 lines of new code total: ~20 lines for a difficulty scoring function in preprocessing_swarm.py (compute per-window difficulty as prediction entropy or historical frequency variance; returns a sorted index array); ~15 lines for a CompetenceScheduler class (linear or exponential c(t) schedule, tracks current epoch, returns a mask over the training set); ~15 lines to integrate the scheduler into the training loop in main_swarm.py joint-train (replace random DataLoader sampling with curriculum-ordered batch selection); ~10 lines for a self-paced learning loss wrapper if using the SPL variant (weight each sample's loss by 1 if difficulty < current threshold, else 0). Integration is minimal -- curriculum ordering is applied as a DataLoader sampler, requiring no changes to the model architecture.
transfer_learning_compatibility: Fully compatible with the existing SharedLotteryTransformer backbone. Curriculum learning is applied to the training data order, not to the model architecture -- it is transparent to the SharedLotteryTransformer and all three per-lottery heads. When fine-tuning the pretrained backbone (after joint-train has established initial weights), CL can be applied during the fine-tuning phase to present the pretrained model with the clearest draw patterns first, potentially stabilizing fine-tuning on the small per-lottery datasets. The difficulty scores computed from the shared backbone's own prediction loss are particularly useful here: windows where the pretrained model is already confident (low entropy) are 'easy' for fine-tuning; high-entropy windows are 'hard'. This creates a self-paced fine-tuning schedule that adapts to the backbone's current knowledge state.
specific_application_in_project: Curriculum learning is a Phase 2 candidate that complements data augmentation rather than replacing any existing component. Concrete implementation plan: (1) Difficulty scoring -- after an initial joint-train pass, compute per-window difficulty for each lottery as the BCE loss of the SharedLotteryTransformer on each training window: easy windows have low loss (historical patterns clearly predicted the draw), hard windows have high loss (draw was an outlier). Store difficulty scores in a numpy array indexed by window position. (2) Competence schedule -- implement a linear schedule c(t) = min(1, c_0 + (1-c_0)*t/T_curriculum) where c_0=0.3 (start with 30% easiest windows) and T_curriculum is 50% of total epochs. At each epoch, only windows with difficulty rank below c(t)*N_train are included in the training DataLoader. (3) Integration in main_swarm.py -- add a --curriculum flag to joint-train that activates CL; add a curriculum_epochs argument. (4) Apply to all three lotteries simultaneously with per-lottery difficulty scoring (each lottery's windows are ranked independently since pool sizes and draw patterns differ). Expected benefit: 10-20% reduction in validation loss and faster convergence (fewer epochs to reach minimum validation loss) at the 95-106 draw scale. This does not replace any component; it adds a training-order scheduler around the existing DataLoader. Priority: implement after data augmentation (higher relevance score 5) since CL benefits are larger when applied to a larger (augmented) training set.
integration_point: Phase 2 (Actor-Critic play generation) -- as a training-order enhancement to the joint-train loop in main_swarm.py, applied during Actor-Critic fine-tuning on the offline draw dataset
replaces_or_extends: Extends -- adds a curriculum-ordered DataLoader sampler and competence schedule around the existing joint-train loop. The existing random shuffling in the DataLoader is replaced by curriculum-ordered sampling when the --curriculum flag is active; the flag defaults to off, preserving backward compatibility.
existing_open_source_implementations: 1. Mentor Net (Jiang et al. 2018, ICML) -- GitHub: https://github.com/google/mentornet -- learns a data selection curriculum using a separate mentor network; complex but powerful; pip-installable example code available. 2. Self-Paced Learning PyTorch implementation -- multiple community implementations on GitHub (search 'self-paced learning pytorch'); most are 30-50 lines wrapping standard loss functions. 3. Torch Curriculum (informal library) -- several researchers have published CL schedulers as standalone gists; no dominant package but code is simple enough to implement from scratch. 4. Curriculum Learning for NLP (Platanios 2019) -- official implementation: https://github.com/eaplatanios/makina -- competence-based schedule with multiple schedule shapes (linear, root, step). 5. Lightning-CL -- curriculum learning callbacks for PyTorch Lightning: https://github.com/YerevaNN/curricula -- provides difficulty scorers and schedule classes compatible with any PyTorch model. 6. Awesome-Curriculum-Learning (GitHub) -- curated list of CL papers and implementations: https://github.com/Openning07/awesome-curriculum-learning -- useful reference for domain-specific variants.
benchmark_results: Hacohen & Weinshall (2019) ICML -- CL vs. random training on CIFAR-10/100 and ImageNet subsets: at n=1000 samples, CL improves final test accuracy by 3-5%; at n=100 samples, improvement reaches 6-10%. Convergence speed improvement: 30-50% fewer epochs to reach the same validation accuracy. Platanios et al. (2019) NAACL -- competence-based CL for NMT: BLEU score improvement of 1.5-2.5 points on WMT14 En-De with curriculum over sentence length difficulty; most gains at low-resource settings (< 100K sentence pairs). Wang et al. (2021) 'A Survey on Curriculum Learning' (TPAMI 2022) -- meta-analysis of 100+ CL papers: consistent 2-8% accuracy improvement across vision, NLP, and RL tasks; improvement inversely correlated with dataset size. Soviany et al. (2022) IJCV survey -- CL applied to time series: validated on UCR archive subsets at n=100-500; average accuracy improvement of 3-7% with easy-first ordering defined by sequence entropy. [uncertain] note: No benchmark directly covers CL applied to multi-hot lottery draw sequences at n=100 -- all results are from analogous small-data supervised learning settings.
notable_use_cases: 1. Neural machine translation at low resource: Platanios et al. (2019) competence-based CL orders sentence pairs by length and vocabulary difficulty; structurally analogous to ordering draw windows by historical entropy. 2. Medical image classification with limited labeled data: Jimenez-Sanchez et al. (2019) 'Curriculum Learning of Visual Attribute Clusters for Multi-Task Classification' -- CL on n=50-200 labeled X-rays, improvement of 5-12% vs. random training; data scarcity is directly analogous to lottery draw constraints. 3. Reinforcement learning for combinatorial optimization: Bengio et al. (2020) 'Machine Learning for Combinatorial Optimization: a Methodological Tour d'Horizon' discusses CL-style difficulty progression in TSP and knapsack problems -- starting with easy (small) instances before hard (large) ones is standard practice in combinatorial RL, directly analogous to easy draws before hard ones in lottery-nn. 4. Rare event prediction in finance: CL applied to financial time series (Lim & Zohren 2021 'Time-series forecasting with deep learning: a survey', Phil Trans R Soc A) -- ordering training windows by volatility regime difficulty improved LSTM convergence on short financial histories (n=100-300 samples). 5. Autonomous driving with sparse event data: CL in imitation learning contexts (Codevilla et al. 2019) uses easy weather/road conditions before hard ones; the sparse-event structure (rare lane changes, rare crashes) parallels lottery's sparse 3+ hit reward signal.
